propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of the RAD decision dismissing the Applicant's appeal of the RPD negative decision.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of a decision made by the Refugee Appeal Division (the RAD) on July 22, 2021, (the Decision) in which the RAD dismissed the Applicant’s appeal of a negative decision made by the Refugee Protection Division (the RPD) on November 3, 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of the RAD decision dismissing the Applicant's appeal of the RPD negative decision.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a Norwegian citizen born in Somalia who entered Canada using a fraudulent or improperly obtained passport.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of Norway who was born in Somalia. She stated that she entered Canada on November 22, 2019 at Vancouver, using a fraudulent or improperly obtained passport that contained a photograph of someone who looked like her.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a Norwegian citizen born in Somalia who entered Canada with a fraudulent or improperly obtained passport.

propositions.text: The Applicant made a refugee claim falsely alleging she fled Somalia after an Al-Shabaab attack weeks earlier.
propositions.quote: Upon entry, the Applicant made a refugee claim based on the false allegation that she had recently fled Somalia after an attack from Al-Shabaab several weeks earlier.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant made a refugee claim falsely alleging recent flight from Somalia after an Al-Shabaab attack.

propositions.text: The RPD held a hearing on October 27, 2020, with the Minister intervening in writing on the Applicant's credibility due to two identities and nondisclosure of Norwegian citizenship.
propositions.quote: The RPD conducted a hearing on October 27, 2020. The Minister intervened in writing, submitting documentary materials concerning the credibility of the Applicant on the basis that she had two identities and initially failed to disclose her status in Norway as a citizen.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD held a hearing with the Minister intervening on the Applicant's credibility due to two identities and nondisclosure of Norwegian citizenship.

propositions.text: The Applicant's refugee claim was based on fear of losing Norwegian citizenship and forced marriage to her cousin in Somalia.
propositions.quote: The Applicant based her refugee claim on a fear of losing her Norwegian citizenship and of being forced to return to Somalia, where she would be forced into marriage with her cousin, the son of her aunt.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant's refugee claim was based on fear of losing Norwegian citizenship and forced marriage in Somalia.

propositions.text: The application is dismissed as the Decision is found reasonable.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, this application is dismissed as I find the Decision is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application, finding the Decision reasonable.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Applicant's identity was a central issue; claim made under name Ikram Mohamed Ahmed, Somali citizen born Dec 25, 1997.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the identity of the Applicant was a central issue. Her refugee claim was made under the name Ikram Mohamed Ahmed, a Somali citizen born on December 25, 1997.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Applicant's identity a central issue; claim made under name Ikram Mohamed Ahmed, born Dec 25, 1997.

propositions.text: Applicant entered Canada Oct 23, 2019 at Toronto using Norwegian passport under name Sabah Abdi Omar, born Jan 20, 1986.
propositions.quote: The evidence established that the Applicant entered Canada on October 23, 2019, at Toronto Pearson Airport using a Norwegian passport under the identity of “Sabah Abdi Omar”, born on January 20, 1986.

propositions.text: Applicant initially denied being the person in the passport but identity confirmed by Norwegian authorities via liaison officer.
propositions.quote: Although the Applicant initially denied she was the person in the passport, her photograph and biometrics were sent to a liaison officer who confirmed her identity with Norwegian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Applicant entered Canada Oct 23, 2019 using Norwegian passport under name Sabah Abdi Omar; identity confirmed by Norwegian authorities.

propositions.text: Applicant amended Basis of Claim admitting identity in Norwegian passport, used two names interchangeably, born 1997.
propositions.quote: The Applicant then submitted an amended Basis of Claim (BOC) admitting that she was the person in the Norwegian passport. She alleged that she used the two names interchangeably and that she was in fact born in 1997.

propositions.text: Applicant alleged aunt sent her to Norway in 2010 to work and send money, claiming to be adult though only 13 years old.
propositions.quote: She alleged that she was sent to Norway in 2010 by her aunt to work and send money back to Somalia. To do so, her aunt made her claim to be an adult in her asylum claim when she was, in fact, only 13 years old.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant amended claim admitting identity, used two names, born 1997; alleged aunt sent her to Norway in 2010 claiming adult though only 13.

propositions.text: Applicant feared mistreatment from aunt who threatened to expose her to Norwegian authorities if she refused marriage to aunt's son.
propositions.quote: The Applicant claimed before the RPD that she feared mistreatment from the aunt who threatened to expose her to the Norwegian authorities if she did not agree to marry her son for immigration purposes.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant feared mistreatment from aunt threatening exposure to Norwegian authorities if she refused marriage to aunt's son.

propositions.text: Applicant explained she was given name Ikram Mohamed Ahmed at birth and later took stepfather's name, known by both in Mogadishu.
propositions.quote: The Applicant explained before the RPD that she was given the name Ikram Mohamed Ahmed at birth. When her mother remarried the Applicant was given the name of her mother’s new husband. She was known by each of these identities while growing up in Mogadishu.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant explained she had birth name Ikram Mohamed Ahmed and later took stepfather's name, known by both in Mogadishu.

propositions.text: RPD found Applicant's testimony credible and accepted amended BOC as truth, including aunt's threats and sending to Norway at 13.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Applicant’s overall testimony to be credible and accepted the Applicant’s amended BOC as the truth. The Panel found it credible that the Applicant’s aunt sent her to Norway to send money back since the age of 13 and threatened to force her to return to Somalia to marry her son so that the son could move to Norway and benefit from the Applicant’s status there.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Applicant credible and accepted amended BOC, including aunt's threats and sending her to Norway at 13.

propositions.text: Claim failed on well-founded fear of persecution in Norway; misrepresentation under Norwegian law unlikely to cause loss of citizenship.
propositions.quote: However, the claim failed on establishing a well-founded fear of persecution in Norway. The RPD reviewed the Norwegian Nationality Act contained in the NDP and held that although misrepresentation under the Act can lead to fines or, less likely, imprisonment, there is “insufficient information to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would lose her citizenship in Norway due to the fact that she gave her second name and an alternate birth date to authorities when she made her claim in 2010.”

paragraphs.summary: RPD found claim failed on fear of persecution in Norway; misrepresentation unlikely to cause loss of citizenship.

propositions.text: RPD denied refugee claim, found Applicant not a Convention Refugee or person in need of protection; noted limited evidence due to self-representation.
propositions.quote: The RPD denied the Applicant’s refugee claim and determined that she was not a Convention Refugee nor a person in need of protection. In the course of doing so, the RPD noted that the evidence before the panel was limited due to the Applicant’s self-representation.

paragraphs.summary: RPD denied refugee claim, found Applicant not a Convention Refugee or protected person; noted limited evidence due to self-representation.

propositions.text: Applicant appealed to RAD with counsel; RAD upheld RPD decision but on different grounds.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, with the assistance of counsel, appealed to the RAD, which upheld the decision of the RPD but on different grounds.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant appealed to RAD with counsel; RAD upheld RPD decision on different grounds.

propositions.text: RAD requested further submissions on identity, misrepresentation, and credibility issues on appeal.
propositions.quote: By way of letter dated March 29, 2021, the RAD requested further submissions on the following issues to be considered on appeal: Whether the RPD reached the correct determination with respect to the Appellant’s identity, including her name and date of birth; Whether the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant had misrepresented her identity in Norway through the influence of an aunt; Whether the Appellant’s evidence is credible, in light of the information contained in the Minister’s intervention.

paragraphs.summary: RAD requested further submissions on identity, misrepresentation, and credibility issues on appeal.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted new evidence including legal opinion, letters of support, Norwegian travel document, and untranslated asylum documents.
propositions.quote: The Applicant provided further submissions on these issues and submitted the following new evidence: A legal opinion from Felix Olivier Helle, an asylum lawyer in Norway; A letter of support from the Applicant’s family friend, who lives in the US; A letter of support from the Applicant’s maternal uncle, who lives in Ethiopia; A copy of the Applicant’s Norwegian travel document; and, Various untranslated documents from the Applicant’s Norwegian asylum file.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submitted new evidence including legal opinion, letters of support, Norwegian travel document, and untranslated asylum documents.

propositions.text: RAD admitted all evidence except untranslated documents, which did not comply with Rule 28 of RAD Rules.
propositions.quote: The RAD admitted all the evidence except the untranslated documents, which did not comply with Rule 28 of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules.

paragraphs.summary: RAD admitted all evidence except untranslated documents, which did not comply with Rule 28 of RAD Rules.

propositions.text: RAD found oral hearing unnecessary as no new discrepancies or contradictions required explanation from Applicant.
propositions.quote: Although an oral hearing was requested, the RAD found one was not necessary because, although the Applicant’s credibility was at issue, there were no discrepancies in the new evidence that the Applicant was not already aware of, nor any contradictions that needed to be put to the Applicant for an explanation.

propositions.text: RAD's task was to conduct independent assessment and weigh the evidence.
propositions.quote: As such, the RAD found that their task was to conduct an independent assessment and weigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found oral hearing unnecessary as no new discrepancies existed; task was to independently assess and weigh evidence.

propositions.text: RAD conducted independent analysis using correctness standard per Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93.
propositions.quote: The RAD conducted an independent analysis using the correctness standard as required by the Federal Court of Appeal in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93.

paragraphs.summary: RAD conducted independent analysis using correctness standard per Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93.

propositions.text: The RAD determined the Applicant is Sabah Abdi Omar, born January 20, 1986, per her Norwegian travel document.
propositions.quote: The RAD determined that the Applicant is Sabah Abdi Omar, born on January 20, 1986, as indicated in her Norwegian travel document.

propositions.text: The RAD found the Applicant untrustworthy and placed no weight on her unsupported claims of misrepresenting name and age to Norwegian authorities.
propositions.quote: Although the Applicant claimed to have misrepresented her name and age to the Norwegian authorities, the RAD determined she was an untrustworthy witness and placed no weight on her unsupported statements.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the Applicant's identity as per Norwegian document and rejected her claims of misrepresentation as untrustworthy (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The RAD questioned the RPD's acceptance of Applicant's testimony despite serious credibility concerns and false statements to immigration officials.
propositions.quote: The RAD questioned the RPD’s acceptance of the Applicant’s testimony in the face of the serious credibility concerns and false statements made to immigration officials.

propositions.text: No evidence existed of remittances or communications between Applicant and her aunt or credible evidence of aunt's influence from afar.
propositions.quote: There was no evidence of remittances sent to the Applicant’s aunt, nor of any communications between them or any other credible evidence about the influence on the Applicant of her aunt, from a continent away.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD doubted RPD's acceptance of Applicant's testimony due to credibility issues and lack of evidence about aunt's influence (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Applicant's explanations about aunt and identity misrepresentations arose only after Canadian immigration caught misrepresentations.
propositions.quote: The RAD noted that the Applicant’s explanations about her aunt and the misrepresentations of her identity in Norway only arose after her misrepresentations to Canadian immigration officers were caught.

propositions.text: Applicant's testimony, affidavit, and new support letters insufficient to overcome credibility issues; RAD did not accept identity misrepresentation claim in Norway.
propositions.quote: The RAD concluded that the Applicant’s testimony, affidavit and the new letters of support submitted were insufficient to overcome the credibility issues and did not accept that she misrepresented her identity in Norway.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Applicant's explanations arose post-detection and were insufficient to overcome credibility issues (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: RAD addressed Applicant's claim of risk of losing Norwegian citizenship and deportation to Somalia, emphasizing identity not based on misrepresentations.
propositions.quote: With respect to the Applicant’s risk of persecution in Norway, the RAD addressed the Applicant’s claim that she would lose her citizenship in Norway and would likely be deported to Somalia. The RAD emphasized its conclusion that the Applicant’s identity in Norway was not based on misrepresentations.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD considered Applicant's risk claims but emphasized identity was not misrepresented (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Applicant argued citizenship revocation risk due to Norwegian belief of fraudulent asylum claim and targeting of Somalis who sought asylum around same time.
propositions.quote: The RAD considered the Applicant’s argument that her citizenship remains susceptible to revocation because Norwegian authorities will believe that her asylum claim was fraudulent. The Applicant argued that this is part of a pattern of targeting of Somalis who successfully sought asylum in Norway around the same time as the Applicant’s arrival.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argued citizenship revocation risk due to perceived fraudulent asylum and targeting of Somalis (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: RAD found RPD erred in concluding revocation unlikely; Norwegian Nationality Act allows revocation for material misrepresentations.
propositions.quote: The RAD independently assessed the Norwegian Nationality Act and found that the RPD had erred in its conclusion that revocation was not likely on a balance of probabilities. Section 26 of the Norwegian Nationality Act states that a revocation of citizenship can occur for material representations.

propositions.text: Legal opinion of Mr. Helle confirmed citizenship revocation possible for fraudulent acquisition; Norwegian authorities increasingly pursue revocation, especially for Somalis arriving 2008-2011.
propositions.quote: This was confirmed by the legal opinion of Mr. Helle, who stated that a person who has fraudulently acquired Norwegian citizenship may subsequently have it revoked. Mr. Helle further stated that based on his experience as a practicing immigration and refugee lawyer in Norway, Norwegian immigration authorities are increasingly working on revocation, cessation and expulsion cases, particularly for Somalis who arrived in Norway between 2008 to 2011.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found RPD erred; Norwegian law allows revocation for fraud; Mr. Helle confirmed increased revocation efforts for Somalis (earlier decision-maker, witness).

propositions.text: Mr. Helle opined Applicant's case at heightened risk due to sparse asylum details, inconsistent allegations, little family knowledge, small maternal family, flight payment discrepancies, and sibling info inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: Mr. Helle opined that the Applicant’s case may be at a heightened risk of reassessment for the following reasons: The information in the Appellant's file about her reasons for seeking asylum contains very few details; Her allegations are not consistent with information about the situation in Mogadishu in 2009, such as whether Al-Shabaab members would have given women a warning before kidnapping them; She had little knowledge of her family and clan, which is considered unusual for Somalis, especially from the Hawiye clan; The size of the Appellant's family on her mother's side seems small given the average number of children per woman in Somalia; There were discrepancies in the Appellant's description of how she paid for her flight; and, She gave inconsistent information to authorities about whether she had any siblings.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Helle opined Applicant's case at heightened risk due to multiple inconsistencies and sparse details (witness).

propositions.text: RAD determined Norway's enforcement of citizenship and immigration laws does not constitute persecution on a Convention ground.
propositions.quote: However, the RAD determined that Norway’s enforcement of its citizenship and immigration laws does not constitute persecution on a Convention ground.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found Norway's enforcement of laws is not persecution on a Convention ground (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: RAD found deportation possibility speculative; revocation does not automatically cause deportation, referencing Mr. Helle's letter on proportionality assessments.
propositions.quote: Referencing Mr. Helle’s letter that both the revocation and deportation proceedings involved proportionality assessments, the RAD found that the possibility of deportation to Somalia remains speculative and the revocation of citizenship does not automatically result in deportation.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found deportation speculative and revocation not automatic deportation, citing Mr. Helle (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Only 17% of Somali cases resulted in revocation; affected individuals may still get resident permits with correct info.
propositions.quote: Additionally, the RAD found that only 17% of Somali cases resulted in revocation and affected individuals may still acquire a resident permit on the basis of correct information.

paragraphs.summary: RAD noted 17% Somali cases had revocation; affected persons may still get resident permits (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: All foreigners in Norway protected by non-refoulement principle regardless of status; removal to Somalia violating this is speculative.
propositions.quote: Finally, the RAD noted that all foreigners in Norway are protected by the principle of non-refoulement regardless of their legal status. Therefore, the prospect of the Applicant’s removal to Somalia, in violation of this principle, remains speculative.

paragraphs.summary: RAD noted non-refoulement protects all foreigners; removal violating it is speculative (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: RAD disagreed with RPD on identity and citizenship revocation risk; concluded Applicant failed to establish well-founded fear of persecution or risk of torture in Norway; confirmed RPD's negative decision and dismissed appeal.
propositions.quote: Overall, the RAD disagreed with the RPD’s conclusion on the Applicant’s identity and possibility of citizenship revocation in Norway and concluded that she failed to establish a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground in Norway or a danger of torture, risk to life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Norway. As such, the RPD’s negative decision was confirmed and the appeal was dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: RAD disagreed with RPD on identity and revocation risk; found no well-founded fear; confirmed RPD's negative decision and dismissed appeal (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The only issue is whether the Decision is reasonable.
propositions.quote: The only issue in this application is whether the Decision is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the sole issue is whether the Decision is reasonable (court).

propositions.text: Applicant relies on five sub-issues to show unreasonableness: failure to defer to RPD credibility, failure to benefit from presumption of truth, little weight to psychological report, refusal of oral hearing, speculation on citizenship loss and removal risk.
propositions.quote: The Applicant relies on five sub-issues to show the Decision is unreasonable. These are: the RAD failed to show deference to the RPD’s credibility findings; the Applicant failed to benefit from the presumption of truth; the RAD improperly afforded little weight to the Applicant’s psychological report; the RAD refused to hold an oral hearing; the RAD speculated regarding the Applicant’s risk of losing her citizenship in Norway and being removed from Norway to Somalia.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Decision unreasonable on five grounds including deference, presumption of truth, psychological report, oral hearing, and speculation on risks (applicant).

propositions.text: Vavilov confirmed judicial review standard is reasonableness, burden on challenger to show unreasonableness; exceptions not applying here.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] extensively reviewed the law of judicial review of administrative decisions. It confirmed that judicial review of an administrative decision is presumed to be on the standard of reasonableness, subject to certain exceptions which do not apply on these facts, and the burden is on the party challenging the decision to show it is unreasonable: Vavilov at paras 23 and 100; Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Huruglica 2016 FCA 93 at para 35 [Huruglica].

paragraphs.summary: Vavilov confirms judicial review standard is reasonableness with burden on challenger; exceptions not applying here (prior court).

propositions.text: Reasonable decision shows justification, transparency, intelligibility; serious shortcomings needed to set aside decision.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is one that displays justification, transparency and intelligibility with a focus on the decision actually made, including the reasons offered for it. To set a decision aside, a reviewing court must be satisfied that there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency: Vavilov at para 100.

paragraphs.summary: Reasonable decision must show justification, transparency, intelligibility; serious flaws needed to set aside (prior court).

propositions.text: Reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, justified by facts and law constraining decision-maker.
propositions.quote: Overall, a reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker: Vavilov at paras 15 and 85.

paragraphs.summary: Reasonable decision is coherent, rational, and justified by facts and law (prior court).

propositions.text: RAD's role is to intervene if RPD is wrong in law, fact, or both; RAD reviews RPD decision applying correctness standard.
propositions.quote: The role of the RAD is to intervene when the RPD is wrong in law, in fact, or in fact and law. The RAD is required to review the decision of the RPD by applying the correctness standard Huruglica at para 78.

paragraphs.summary: Court states RAD intervenes if RPD wrong in law or fact, reviewing under correctness standard (court).

propositions.text: Applicant submitted RAD owed deference to RPD's credibility findings due to RPD's benefit of in-person credibility testing.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submitted to the RAD that it owed deference to the RPD’s credibility findings because the RPD had the benefit of testing the Applicant’s credibility in person.

propositions.text: RAD found deference owed only where RPD had meaningful advantage in assessing evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD reviewed the jurisprudence and found that “[d]eference is owed to the RPD only where the RPD held a meaningful advantage in assessing the evidence.”

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argued RAD owed deference to RPD's credibility findings; RAD found deference only if RPD had meaningful advantage (applicant, earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Rozas del Solar established deference to RPD is case-by-case; RAD must determine if RPD had advantageous position and if RAD can decide claim.
propositions.quote: It was established by Mr. Justice Diner in Rozas del Solar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 1145 [Rozas del Solar] at paragraph 134 that the degree of deference owed to the RPD “ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis. In each case, the RAD ought to determine whether the RPD truly benefited from an advantageous position, and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final decision in respect of the refugee claim”.

paragraphs.summary: Rozas del Solar held deference to RPD is case-by-case; RAD must assess RPD's advantage and ability to decide claim (prior court).

propositions.text: The RAD reviewed the RPD’s written record and full audio recording of the hearing.
propositions.quote: Here, the RAD reviewed the RPD’s written record and the full audio recording of the RPD hearing.

propositions.text: The RAD found no indication the audio recording failed to capture the hearing.
propositions.quote: The RAD noted that “there is no indication that the contents of the audio recording do not capture what occurred at the hearing.”

propositions.text: The RAD concluded it would apply a correctness standard to the RPD findings, not deference.
propositions.quote: The RAD concluded that there was no reason to show deference to any of the RPD findings and a correctness standard would be applied by the RAD to the RPD findings.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reviewed the RPD record and audio, found no indication of incompleteness, and applied correctness standard to RPD findings (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: When RAD reviews audio recordings and written record, it may find no advantage in RPD credibility assessment and make its own determination.
propositions.quote: Where audio recordings of testimony are available and reviewed by the RAD in addition to the written record and the RPD’s conclusions, it is reasonable for the RAD to find no meaningful advantage in the assessment of credibility, and to make its own determination: Rozas del Solar at paras 89-90.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD may disregard RPD credibility advantage when it reviews audio and written records and make its own decision (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: The RAD was not required to show deference to the RPD’s credibility findings.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I am satisfied the RAD was not required to show deference to the RPD’s credibility findings.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RAD was not required to defer to the RPD’s credibility findings (court).

propositions.text: The RAD did not give the Applicant the benefit of the presumption of truthfulness.
propositions.quote: The Applicant states that the RAD did not provide her with the benefit of the presumption of truthfulness.

propositions.text: Applicant argues her evidence reasonably explained not declaring Norwegian identity initially, so presumption was not rebutted.
propositions.quote: She says, for example, that it was not rebutted because her evidence provided reasonable explanations for not declaring her Norwegian identity when she first landed in Canada.

propositions.text: Applicant states she was scared and traumatized by her aunt but eventually declared truth in amended claim.
propositions.quote: She states that she was scared and traumatized by her aunt, but notes that she eventually declared the truth in the amended basis of claim.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD failed to apply the presumption of truthfulness and her explanations justified nondisclosure (applicant).

propositions.text: The RAD acknowledged the presumption of truthfulness but said it may be rebutted by contradictions, omissions, or implausibilities not reasonably explained.
propositions.quote: The RAD acknowledged the existence of the presumption and noted that it may be rebutted when a valid reason to doubt the truthfulness of the testimony is identified. Examples given of such valid reasons were “a contradiction, omission, or implausibility that is not reasonably explained.”

paragraphs.summary: The RAD recognized the presumption of truthfulness but said it can be rebutted by valid reasons like contradictions or omissions (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: The RAD found serious credibility concerns raised by the Minister were not adequately addressed by the RPD.
propositions.quote: After reviewing several serious credibility concerns that were highlighted in the Minister’s intervention package, the RAD was of the view that those concerns were not adequately addressed by the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the RPD did not adequately address serious credibility concerns raised by the Minister (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: The RAD noted inconsistent and evolving statements about Applicant’s identity, including fabricated story and omissions.
propositions.quote: The RAD noted there were inconsistent and evolving statements about the Applicant’s identity, which were highly concerning. The story told in her original BOC was fictitious as she had fabricated her story. The Applicant had omitted entirely the fact that she relocated to Norway in 2010 although she claimed to have fled Somalia in 2019.

propositions.text: Applicant denied past fingerprinting and living outside Somalia and Kenya, then denied Norwegian passport name was hers.
propositions.quote: As recently as January, 2020, the Applicant denied being fingerprinted in the past and continued to claim that she had only ever lived in Somalia and in Kenya. When confronted with the name in the Norwegian passport the Applicant first denied it was her name suggesting it perhaps was the name on the false passport she had used.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Applicant gave inconsistent, fabricated identity statements and denied Norwegian passport name (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: It is unnecessary to review other contradictions and false statements made by the Applicant to immigration officers.
propositions.quote: I find it is not necessary to review the many other contradictions and false statements made by the Applicant to immigration officers.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no need to review other contradictions and false statements by the Applicant (court).

propositions.text: The RAD found the RPD should have been concerned about Applicant’s willingness to deceive about her identity.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the RPD should have been quite concerned about the Applicant’s willingness to deceive and mislead immigration officers as to her identity.

propositions.text: The RPD gave few reasons to justify suddenly believing Applicant’s testimony without corroborative evidence.
propositions.quote: The Board noted that the RPD gave very few reasons to justify why, in the absence of any corroborative evidence, it suddenly believed the Applicant’s testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the RPD should have been concerned about Applicant’s deception and gave few reasons to believe her without evidence (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: The RAD found Applicant’s false statements badly tainted her credibility and rebutted presumption of truthfulness.
propositions.quote: The RAD reasonably found the false statements made by the Applicant badly tainted her credibility and wholly rebutted the presumption of the truthfulness of her testimony: Luo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 823 at paras 18-22.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Applicant’s false statements destroyed her credibility and rebutted the presumption of truthfulness (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: Applicant argues it is unreasonable to afford little weight to psychological report solely because psychologist lacked firsthand knowledge.
propositions.quote: To support the proposition that the RAD improperly afforded little weight to the Applicant’s psychological report the Applicant refers to cases finding that it is unreasonable to afford little weight to a psychological report solely on the basis that the events it described were not based on firsthand knowledge of the psychologist and it is an error to reject expert psychological evidence without any basis.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues it is unreasonable to give little weight to psychological reports lacking psychologist’s firsthand knowledge (applicant).

propositions.text: The RAD did not place little weight on psychological evaluation but found diagnoses had little bearing on forward-looking risk.
propositions.quote: The RAD did not place little weight on the psychological evaluation. The RAD acknowledged the Applicant’s diagnoses of post-traumatic stress disorder and major depressive disorder, as well as the recommended treatment plan. The RAD found however that the Applicant’s diagnoses had little bearing on her forward-looking risk in Norway such that it would entitle her to refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD acknowledged psychological diagnoses but found they had little bearing on refugee protection risk (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: No reviewable error in RAD’s treatment of psychological evaluation; disagreement on weight is not reviewable.
propositions.quote: I find that there is no reviewable error in the RAD’s treatment of the psychological evaluation. The Applicant’s argument appears merely to be a disagreement with the weight assigned to this evidence by the RAD. It is well know that this is an exercise from which the Court must refrain on judicial review: Vavilov at para 125.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no reviewable error in RAD’s treatment of psychological evidence; weight disagreements are not reviewable (court).

propositions.text: The RAD found little reason to hold an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) as new evidence did not meet criteria.
propositions.quote: The RAD found there was little reason to hold an oral hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 as the new evidence does not meet any of the criteria found in subsection 110(6).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found no reason to hold an oral hearing as new evidence did not meet subsection 110(6) criteria (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: New evidence did not raise serious credibility issues or affect refugee claim decision; lacked probative value.
propositions.quote: The new evidence did not raise a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Applicant. Nor would it be central to the decision with respect to the Applicant’s refugee protection claim. In particular, the RAD found that accepting the new evidence would not justify allowing or rejecting the Applicant’s claim as it lacks probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found new evidence lacked probative value and did not raise serious credibility or claim issues (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: After reviewing RPD record and audio, RAD found new evidence did not raise new contradictions or discrepancies.
propositions.quote: After reviewing the RPD record and the audio recording, the RAD determined that the new evidence did not raise any contradictions or discrepancies that had not already been put to the Applicant. The only remaining step was to weigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found new evidence did not raise new contradictions beyond those already addressed (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: Applicant had opportunity to respond to RAD’s concerns based on Minister’s intervention; concerns were known to Applicant.
propositions.quote: The Applicant was provided with an opportunity to respond to the RAD’s concerns as expressed in the letter dated March 29, 2021. Those concerns were largely based on the Minister’s intervention at the RPD. The RAD found that the Applicant should have been well aware of those existing credibility concerns.

propositions.text: No error found in RAD’s reasoning about Applicant’s awareness of credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: I do not find any error with this reasoning.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD gave Applicant opportunity to respond to known credibility concerns; court finds no error in this reasoning (earlier_decision_maker, court).

propositions.text: RAD met its onus to consider oral hearing request and analyzed subsection 110(6) criteria.
propositions.quote: I find the RAD met its onus to carefully consider the Applicant’s request for an oral hearing and it demonstrated, through its reasons, an analysis of the subsection 110(6) criteria.

propositions.text: This case differs from Tchangoue and Hundal where authenticity or new contradictory evidence justified oral hearing.
propositions.quote: This was not an instance where the authenticity of documents was in question as in Tchangoue v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 334 at paragraph 17, nor were the RAD’s adverse credibility findings based on new evidence that directly contradicted the RPD’s findings as in Hundal v Canada ((Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 72 at paragraph 20.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD properly considered oral hearing request and this case differs from precedents requiring oral hearings (court).

propositions.text: Applicant argues psychological report was new evidence enhancing her credibility.
propositions.quote: As the Applicant states in her memoranda, the psychological report submitted before the RAD was new evidence that enhanced the credibility of the Applicant.

propositions.text: Even if true, this does not raise new issues or contradictions necessitating an oral hearing.
propositions.quote: While this may have been true, it does not constitute a new issue or raise new contradictions/discrepancies that would necessitate an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues psychological report enhanced credibility; court finds it does not justify oral hearing (applicant, court).

propositions.text: RAD’s independent assessment overturned RPD findings on credibility and identity.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s independent assessment of the RPD record and its own conclusions on the Applicant’s credibility and identity overturned the findings of the RPD.

propositions.text: Applicant had opportunity to address identity and credibility concerns orally at RPD and in written submissions to RAD.
propositions.quote: The Applicant had the opportunity to address the existing concerns of identity and credibility orally at the RPD hearing and again through written submissions upon notice from the RAD.

propositions.text: Concerns about identity and credibility were not unknown to the Applicant.
propositions.quote: These concerns were not unknown to the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD overturned RPD findings; Applicant had opportunity to address concerns which were known to her (earlier_decision_maker).

propositions.text: The RAD did not err in refusing to hold an oral hearing.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the RAD did not err in refusing to hold an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD did not err in refusing to hold an oral hearing.

propositions.text: The Applicant's argument relies on a Norwegian lawyer's legal opinion about citizenship revocation procedures and likely removal from Norway.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s argument here is based on a legal opinion from a lawyer in Norway, Felix Olivier Helle (Mr. Helle), which confirmed the procedures for revocation of citizenship.

propositions.text: The legal opinion states a proportionality assessment would not favor the Applicant and reassessment would result in removal from Norway.
propositions.quote: The legal opinion was that a proportionality assessment would not go in the Applicant’s favour, and that a reassessment of the Applicant’s case would result in removal from Norway.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues based on a Norwegian lawyer's opinion that revocation procedures and removal from Norway are likely.

propositions.text: The Applicant submits the letter confirms she will lose citizenship and that procedures following revocation are not speculative.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the letter confirms she will lose her citizenship. The Applicant adds that the various procedures following revocation were explored by Mr. Helle and therefore they are not “speculative”.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submits the letter confirms loss of citizenship and that post-revocation procedures are not speculative.

propositions.text: The RAD did not ignore Mr. Helle’s opinion and reasonably found enforcement of citizenship laws not persecutory.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the RAD did not ignore Mr. Helle’s legal opinion. The RAD reasonably determined that it would not be persecutory for Norway to enforce its own citizenship and immigration legislation

propositions.text: Revocation is not automatic; deportation involves proportionality assessments and Norway respects non-refoulement.
propositions.quote: properly noted that revocation was not an automatic process. Any deportation proceedings would involve proportionality assessments. The evidence also showed that Norway was committed to the principle of non-refoulement

propositions.text: Persons losing status may obtain residence permits on other grounds in Norway.
propositions.quote: persons who had lost status were sometimes able to get a residence permit on another ground.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits the RAD considered the legal opinion and found enforcement lawful, revocation not automatic, and Norway respects non-refoulement.

propositions.text: As a Norwegian citizen, the Applicant must prove risk of persecution by Norway.
propositions.quote: As a citizen of Norway, the Applicant must establish that her risk of persecution is against Norway.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant must establish risk of persecution by Norway as a Norwegian citizen.

propositions.text: The RAD found the prospect of removal to Somalia speculative since revocation does not automatically cause deportation.
propositions.quote: The RAD concluded that this prospect remained speculative in the sense that the revocation of citizenship does not automatically result in deportation.

propositions.text: The RAD determined Norway's enforcement of citizenship laws is not persecution on a Convention ground.
propositions.quote: The RAD determined that Norway’s enforcement of citizenship and immigration laws does not constitute persecution on a Convention ground.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found removal to Somalia speculative and Norway's enforcement not persecution on a Convention ground.

propositions.text: The RAD's analysis means deportation is possible but involves multiple procedural checkpoints and appeals.
propositions.quote: I do not read the RAD’s analysis on this point to mean that there is no possibility of deportation to Somalia, but that, much like Canada’s immigration system, there are a number of checkpoints the Applicant can access between any loss of status and removal.

propositions.text: The RAD noted opportunities to appeal and proportionality assessments if false information was provided.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes there is an opportunity to appeal a decision of the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration and both the revocation and deportation proceedings involve proportionality assessments if it is found that false information was originally provided by the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD means deportation is possible but involves appeals and proportionality assessments.

propositions.text: From 2017-2018, only 17% of Somali cases led to revocation; most revocations were dismissed and residence permits possible after revocation.
propositions.quote: from March 2017 to December 2018, only 17% of Somali cases resulted in the revocation of status and a great majority of the revocation cases were dismissed. Further, even after revocation of status, affected individuals are eligible to acquire a resident permit based on the correct information.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found most Somali revocation cases dismissed and residence permits possible after revocation.

propositions.text: Norway is committed to non-refoulement; Mr. Helle did not explain why deportation violating this principle is likely.
propositions.quote: Norway, much like Canada, is committed to the principle of non-refoulement and Mr. Helle’s legal opinion failed to explain why there is a high likelihood that the Applicant would be deported, even in violation of this principle.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Norway respects non-refoulement and Mr. Helle did not show likely deportation violating it.

propositions.text: The RAD thoroughly considered Mr. Helle’s opinion and evidence, concluding removal is not automatic after revocation.
propositions.quote: I find that the RAD thoroughly considered Mr. Helle’s legal opinion as well as the evidence gathered from its own independent analysis, to conclude that removal is not automatic following citizenship revocation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD thoroughly considered the legal opinion and evidence, concluding removal is not automatic.

propositions.text: Removal from Norway to Somalia is possible but too remote to support refugee protection on a Convention ground in Canada.
propositions.quote: while removal from Norway to Somalia may be possible, it remains too remote for consideration as a Convention ground for refugee protection in Canada.

propositions.text: No reason to disturb the RAD’s analysis on this point.
propositions.quote: I can find no reason to disturb the RAD’s analysis on this point.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes removal is too remote for refugee protection and will not disturb the RAD's analysis.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed for all reasons given.
propositions.quote: For all the foregoing reasons, this application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review for all reasons given.

propositions.text: There is no serious question of general importance for certification; the application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: There is no serious question of general importance for certification. JUDGMENT in IMM-6207-21 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application is dismissed. There is no question for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious question for certification and dismisses the application.
